data.howToName: How to scale a recipe by one ingredient
notes: Pick the ingredient that limits you, usually the main one or the one running low.
The factor applies to everything, including the pan size and the cooking time check.
If the factor is awkward, round the other amounts to the nearest spoon.

description: Scale a recipe around the ingredient you have. Enter what the recipe calls for and what you have, and every other amount follows from that factor.

examples.result: The factor is 0.5, so the cake uses 1 cup flour, 1/2 cup sugar, 1 egg, and 1/2 cup butter.
steps: Find the factor from the butter: 1/2 cup have ÷ 1 cup called for = 0.5.
Multiply each amount by 0.5: 2 cups flour become 1 cup, 1 cup sugar becomes 1/2 cup.
Eggs: 2 × 0.5 = 1 egg. The butter itself is now 1/2 cup, which is what you have.
examples.title: A cake needs 1 cup butter, you have 1/2 cup

examples.result: The factor is 0.67, so the soup uses 2 cups broth, 2/3 cup beans, 1 onion, and 2 cloves garlic.
steps: Find the factor from the broth: 4 cups have ÷ 6 cups called for = 0.67.
Multiply each amount by 0.67: 3 cups beans become 2 cups, 1 1/2 onions become 1.
Garlic: 3 cloves × 0.67 = 2 cloves. Round counts to whole numbers.
examples.title: A soup needs 6 cups broth, you have 4 cups

faqs.answer: Divide what you have by what the recipe calls for. If the recipe needs 2 cups of flour and you have 1 cup, the factor is 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5. Multiply every other ingredient by 0.5.
faqs.question: How do I work out the factor from one ingredient?

faqs.answer: The ingredient that limits you: the main ingredient, or the one you are running low on. If the chicken is short, scale by the chicken. If the flour is short, scale by the flour. Everything else follows from that one number.
faqs.question: Which ingredient should I scale by?

faqs.answer: Yes, in both directions. If you have more of an ingredient than the recipe needs, the factor is above 1 and the batch grows. The same rules apply: hold back the leavening a little when scaling up.
faqs.question: Can I scale up by one ingredient too?

faqs.answer: Round to the nearest measurable amount. A factor of 0.67 turns 3 cloves of garlic into 2, and 1 1/2 onions into 1. For cups, round to the nearest eighth. For baking, weigh in grams where you can.
faqs.question: What if the factor gives awkward amounts?

faqs.answer: Yes, and it is the most common reason to scale this way. A recipe that needs 500 g of chicken and a packet that holds 350 g gives a factor of 0.7. Scale everything by 0.7 and the recipe fits the packet.
faqs.question: Can I scale by the amount of meat I have?

faqs.answer: Pick one and stick with it. Scaling by two ingredients at once gives two different factors, and the recipe cannot follow both. Choose the one that is shortest, and let the other one have a little left over.
faqs.question: What if two ingredients are short?

felicityNote: This is the use-up-what-you-have scaling. The flour runs out first in my kitchen, so the flour usually sets the batch.

parts.meaning: The multiplier for every ingredient. Amount you have divided by amount the recipe calls for.
The amount of your limiting ingredient that you actually have.
The amount of that ingredient the recipe asks for.
The amount of one ingredient after scaling.

formula.text: Scale factor = amount you have ÷ amount the recipe calls for. Scaled amount = original amount × scale factor.

howToSteps.name: Pick your limiting ingredient
howToSteps.text: Choose the ingredient that sets the batch size: the main ingredient, or the one you are running low on.

howToSteps.name: Find the factor
howToSteps.text: Divide what you have by what the recipe calls for. One cup of flour against a recipe that needs 2 cups gives a factor of 0.5.

howToSteps.name: Scale everything by that factor
howToSteps.text: Work down the ingredient list and multiply each amount by the factor, including the limiting ingredient itself, which should come out to exactly what you have.

howToSteps.name: Round to measurable amounts
howToSteps.text: Round cups to the nearest eighth and counts to whole numbers. For baking, weigh in grams where you can.

howToSteps.name: Match the pan
howToSteps.text: A smaller batch needs a smaller pan so the depth stays the same. Check for doneness a little early.

lede: When one ingredient sets the batch size, the scale factor comes from it: amount you have divided by amount the recipe calls for. Everything else follows.

title: Scale a Recipe by One Ingredient
tutorial: Most scaling starts with servings: the recipe serves 4, you want 10. But sometimes the servings are not the problem. The problem is the butter. The recipe needs a cup, the fridge has half a cup, and the shops are closed. That is when you scale by one ingredient instead: the factor comes from what you have, not from who is coming to dinner.

The maths is the same shape as any other scaling. Divide what you have by what the recipe calls for. Half a cup of butter against a recipe that needs a cup gives a factor of 0.5. Then multiply every other ingredient by 0.5. The flour halves, the sugar halves, the eggs halve. The butter itself comes out to exactly what you have, which is the point. The scaler above takes the two amounts for your limiting ingredient and works out the factor for you.

Pick the ingredient that actually limits you. Usually that is the main ingredient, or the one you are running low on. If the chicken is short, scale by the chicken. If the flour is short, scale by the flour. If two ingredients are short, pick the shorter one and let the other have a little left over. Scaling by two ingredients at once gives two different factors, and a recipe cannot follow both.

The factor from one ingredient is often awkward: 0.67, 0.7, 0.83. Round the results to amounts you can measure. Cups round to the nearest eighth. Counts round to whole numbers: 3 cloves of garlic at a factor of 0.67 become 2 cloves, not 2.01 cloves. For baking, weigh in grams where you can, because grams stay exact at any factor. A large egg is about 50 g out of the shell, which makes egg maths easy at awkward factors.

This kind of scaling is also the use-it-up scaling. Half a bag of flour, the last of the cream, a packet of chicken that is smaller than the recipe expects: scale the recipe to fit what you have, and nothing goes to waste. What is left over after cooking still needs storing properly, so cool it quickly and get it into the fridge or freezer the same day.
